system: Babylonian bēru (double-hours), the UŠ, and the maṣṣartu (watches of night and day) — Mesopotamia, historical layer only, no living continuation
compiledBy: research agent, Horae Mundi round — data dossier only, no code
framingVersion: docs/FRAMING.md v2 (the quotation amendment), as adopted 2026-07-30
headline: THIS SYSTEM HAS NO RULERS. No cuneiform source known to this compiler assigns a planet, a god, or any other ruling power to a bēru or to a watch. The ruler column for the Babylonian row must render empty on every line. See gaps[0] and honestLimits.
dayStart: SUNSET, for the calendar date. The Babylonian civil/calendrical day begins at sunset and the month begins on the evening the new crescent is first seen [src: brack-bernsen-2020, smith-1969, sachs-hunger-1988, parker-dubberstein-1956]. BUT this does not by itself fix the epoch of the divisions below, and the distinction is load-bearing: (a) the schematic texts state the LENGTH of daylight and of night in minas / UŠ / bēru and never state an epoch instant at all [src: steele-sciamvs-2013, at MUL.APIN II ii 21–42]; (b) the attested running counts in bēru are anchored to the nearest boundary event, not to one daily epoch — '1 KASKAL.GÍD ūmu' = the first double-hour OF THE DAYLIGHT (counted from sunrise) and '1 KASKAL.GÍD GE6' = a double-hour OF THE NIGHT (counted from sunset); an astronomical table has '5 KASKAL.GÍD ME.NIM.A', five double-hours of daylight after sunrise [src: cad-b-beru, at CAD B 210 s.v. bēru A mng. 2a, citing YOS 7 18:5, ABL 108:10, RAcc. 129:1, ACT 200 iv 17]. A continuous 1→12 bēru count running from sunset through the following sunset is NOT attested in any source seen here; do not implement one and call it Babylonian.
divisionRule:
TWO PARALLEL AND INDEPENDENT SCHEMES. Do not nest them.

(1) THE BĒRU — a FIXED, EQUAL, non-seasonal unit. The nychthemeron (daylight + night together) = 12 bēru = 360 UŠ. 1 bēru (Sum. DANNA, logogram KASKAL.GÍD; in Old Akkadian also DA.NA) = 30 UŠ. 1 UŠ = 60 NINDA. Therefore 1 bēru = exactly 2 modern equinoctial hours, 1 UŠ = exactly 4 minutes, 1 NINDA = exactly 4 seconds; the whole day-and-night is exactly 360 UŠ = 24 h regardless of season or latitude [src: steele-sciamvs-2013 at p. 4; breger-2022 at pp. 29–30; cad-b-beru at CAD B 208–211]. The bēru is glossed by the dictionary itself as 'double hour (twelfth part of a full day)' — the FULL day, i.e. the nychthemeron, not the daylight. The same word bēru also means (i) a distance, a 'mile' of over 10 km, and (ii) one twelfth of a circle, i.e. 30° of arc [src: cad-b-beru at CAD B 208, 211]. UŠ likewise doubles as 1° of arc. This triple duty (time / arc / distance) is the reason the system is sexagesimal and the reason it is NOT a seasonal-hour system.

(2) THE MAṢṢARTU (watch) — a SEASONALLY VARYING unit. Daylight is divided into three watches and night into three watches, six in all, each one third of the actual daylight or actual night, so that a watch lengthens and shortens with the season [src: smith-1969; steele-shorttime-2020; divmanual at K.6476 rev. right col. 7'–8']. At equinox, and only there, a watch equals 2 bēru = 60 UŠ = 4 modern hours; away from equinox no watch is a whole number of bēru.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ANY ENGINE: the bēru is arithmetic and needs no astronomy; the watch needs real sunrise and sunset (or a schematic daylight-length scheme, see variants). They must be computed by two different code paths and must never be presented as one nested grid.

TRAP — 'watch' in the MUL.APIN schemes does NOT mean a third. In the MUL.APIN shadow-length and water-clock sections, EN.NUN / maṣṣartu denotes the WHOLE of the daytime or the WHOLE of the night, not one third of it. Reading it as a third (as Neugebauer and Pingree did) breaks the arithmetic. See variants[v-massartu-sense] and contestedPoints[0].

beru.alsoMeans: 30° of arc; a road-distance of over 10 km

mina_of_water.note: in the day-length schemes the whole nychthemeron is 6 minas; weight of water and time are taken as directly proportional [src: steele-sciamvs-2013 at p. 4]

entries.name: bēru 1 (of the night, counted from sunset)
entries.note: Individual bēru have NO names and NO rulers in any source seen here. They are counted as ordinals from the anchoring event. Attested night-count usage: RAcc. 129:1 'at the last double-hour of the night'; Camb. 400:45,47 counts double-hours of night before midnight and before morning. The count is not capped at 6 — under the schematic 2:1 scheme the night at winter solstice runs to 8 bēru.

entries.name: bēru 6 (of the night)
entries.note: The 6+6 split is attested only for the equinox: a Neo-Assyrian letter reports that on 15 Nisannu day and night were equal, six double-hours of daylight and six double-hours of night. Away from equinox the two counts are unequal and the sixth bēru of the night may not exist (summer) or may be followed by a seventh and eighth (winter).

entries.name: bēru 1 (of the daylight, counted from sunrise)
entries.note: Attested daylight-count usage: YOS 7 18:5 and YOS 7 20:13 (Neo-Babylonian, an appearance and an assembly dated 'at the first double-hour of the day'); UCP 9 74 No. 82:13 (bricks made at the first double-hour of the day); ABL 108:10 (Neo-Assyrian, 'when five-sixths of the first double-hour of the day had passed'); RAcc. 132:190 'at one and a half double-hours of the morning'; ACT 200 iv 17 'five double-hours of daylight after sunrise'. NOTE the ABL 108 usage: a bēru is subdivided by simple fractions, which only works because it is a fixed length.

entries.name: bēru 5 (of the daylight)
entries.note: ACT 200 iv 17 and 20 explicitly measure 'five double-hours of daylight after sunrise', so a running count of at least five is attested.

entries.name: bēru 6 (of the daylight)
entries.note: See index 6: the 6+6 split is the equinoctial case only.

entries.name: evening watch (first watch of the night)
entries.quality: unfavourable — 'the evening and the middle watch are not favourable' in a hemerology, KAR 177 iii 38 [src: cad-q-qablitu]. This is a quality of the WATCH, assigned by an omen text; it is not a ruling power and no agent is named.
entries.note: Attested from Old Babylonian on, and in Boğazköy, Middle Babylonian and Standard Babylonian. The dominant use is in celestial divination: eclipse omens specify the watch in which the eclipse began. Lexically fixed as the first of three by the bilingual lists (Lu Excerpt II 88ff.; Igituh short version 117ff.; Antagal C 33ff.; Nabnitu D b 5f.), which give the sequence barārītu – qablītu – šāt urri.

associations.extent: one third of the actual night
associations.personified: Yes — Maqlû I 3 invokes the evening, middle and dawn watches by name alongside the gods of the night; Maqlû I 30 and KAR 58 r. 12 address 'the three watches of the night' as wakeful, watchful, restless, sleepless beings. They are addressed, never described as ruling anything. Do NOT promote this to a ruler column.
associations.divinatoryUse: eclipse-timing (ABL 1006:3 = Thompson Rep. 268 states that the evil of an eclipse depends on the month, the day and the watch)

entries.name: middle watch of the night
entries.quality: unfavourable — KAR 177 iii 38, with the evening watch [src: cad-q-qablitu]
entries.note: Attested Old Assyrian / Old Babylonian on. Uses beyond divination: ARM 10 91 r. 5 (someone spoke in the middle watch); Gilgameš V iii 8 / V iv 8 (he ended his sleep in the middle watch); Labat TDP 160:32 (an illness recurring in the middle watch); CT 38 26:37 (a ghost crying in the middle watch); KAR 212 iii 47 (fire breaking out).

associations.extent: one third of the actual night
associations.midnightMarker: 'mišil maṣṣarti', the middle of the watch, is used as a time-marker in Atra-ḫasīs I 70 and 72, and Labat TDP 190:28 reckons 'from the beginning of the night to the middle of the watch' [src: cad-m1-massartu]

entries.name: morning watch (last watch of the night)
entries.quality: propitious — 'the morning watch is favourable' (magrat), KAR 177 iii 39 [src: cad-uw-saturri]. Again a quality of the watch, not an agent.
entries.note: TWO NAMES FOR ONE WATCH, both Tier A, and they are not interchangeable across genres: šāt urri is the ordinary term in omen, medical and ritual texts and in the lexical sequence; namāritu ('dawn', EN.NUN.ZALAG.GA) is used in Maqlû I 3 and in Labat TDP 14:74f. [src: cad-n1-namaritu]. Keep both; do not collapse them.

associations.extent: one third of the actual night
associations.land: Elam — 'the morning watch (concerns) Elam', Thompson Rep. 242 rev. 2, and again ACh Supp. 2 Sin 19:13; and Thompson Rep. 181:6 'the morning watch pertains to Elam, this portent came at sunrise' [src: cad-uw-saturri, cad-s2-seru]. THIS IS THE CLOSEST THING IN THE CORPUS TO AN ASSOCIATION-PER-DIVISION, AND IT IS A LAND, NOT A PLANET OR A GOD. No matching land is attested here for the evening or middle watch — see gaps.
associations.ritualUse: BBR No. 1–20:69 and 149 place an offering 'during the sunlight of the morning watch'; Bab. 4 104:13 has a gift offered in the morning watch [src: cad-uw-saturri]

entries.name: morning watch of the daytime
entries.quality: unattested — the duplicate K.6476 lists the day watches but records no favourable/unfavourable value for them
entries.note: The three DAY watches are the least-known half of this system and are easy to miss. They are attested as a set in the Babylonian Diviner's Manual duplicate K.6476 (rev., right col.), which lists EN.NUN dUSAN / EN.NUN.MURUB₄.BA / EN.NUN U[D.ZAL.LI] as 'the watches of the whole night', and immediately after, en.nun še-rim / en.nun an.ne / en.nun li-la-[a-ti] as 'the watches of the whole day' [src: divmanual; also cited at cad-s2-seru and cad-m1-massartu].

associations.extent: one third of the actual daylight

entries.name: midday watch of the daytime
entries.note: AN.NE is read muṣlālu, 'midday, afternoon, siesta time' [src: cad-m2-muslalu].

associations.extent: one third of the actual daylight

entries.name: evening watch of the daytime
entries.note: lilâtu is 'evening', logogram KIN.SIG [src: cad-l-lilatu]. Note the name collision: the FIRST night watch (barārītu) is also 'the evening watch' in English. Two different divisions. A comparison table that prints both must disambiguate, or it will look like a duplicate row.

variants.label: Real sky versus the ideal 360-day calendar — the first fork, and the one an engine must choose
variants.authority: Both are attested. The schematic scheme is what the surviving TABLES compute; real sunrise/sunset is what the DIARIES and letters observe.
variants.arithmetic: Schematic: the year is twelve 30-day months = 360 days; equinoxes and solstices fall on the 15th of Months I, IV, VII and X; daylight and night lengths run on a linear zigzag between fixed solstitial extremes and never depend on latitude. Observational: daylight and night are whatever the sun actually does at the place. A Horae Mundi engine computing real sunrise/sunset at an arbitrary city is doing something the Babylonian tables never did, and the page must say so.

variants.label: The 2:1 daylight ratio (longest day : shortest day)
variants.authority: The older and much the more widely attested scheme: Enūma Anu Enlil 14, MUL.APIN, the 'Astrolabes', and many later tablets.
variants.arithmetic: Longest daylight (15/IV) = 240 UŠ = 8 bēru = 16 h; shortest daylight (15/X) = 120 UŠ = 4 bēru = 8 h; equinox 180/180 UŠ. Daily change 0;40 UŠ (= 120 UŠ spread over the 180 days between solstices); monthly change 20 UŠ. It is very inaccurate for the latitude of Babylon or anywhere else in Babylonia or Assyria.

variants.label: The 3:2 daylight ratio
variants.authority: Appears only in the System A and System B lunar theories and on BM 29371 and BM 33564. Brown, Fermor and Walker date its arrival to the eighth century BC; Steele cautions that the earliest actual evidence is the late-sixth-century BM 29371, and that the 2:1 ratio went on being used long after 3:2 was known.
variants.arithmetic: Longest daylight = 216 UŠ (3,36) = 14 h 24 m; shortest = 144 UŠ (2,24) = 9 h 36 m; equinox 180/180. Monthly change 12 UŠ.

variants.label: What EN.NUN / maṣṣartu means inside the MUL.APIN schemes
variants.authority: Current reading (Gehlken 1991; Brown, Fermor and Walker 1999–2000; adopted by Steele 2013): in the MUL.APIN shadow-length and day-length statements, 'watch' means the WHOLE of the daytime or the WHOLE of the night. Superseded reading (Neugebauer 1975; Pingree in Hunger–Pingree 1989, and still partly in Hunger–Pingree 1999): it means one THIRD.
variants.arithmetic: Under the current reading, 'on the 15th of Month I, 3 minas is a daytime watch, 3 minas is a nighttime watch' means daylight = 3 minas = 180 UŠ and night = 3 minas = 180 UŠ, total 6 minas = 360 UŠ. Under the superseded reading the same line would mean a THIRD of daylight = 3 minas, i.e. daylight = 9 minas, and the whole scheme fails to close. An engine that implements the superseded reading will be out by a factor of three.

variants.label: Where a bēru count starts
variants.authority: Attested usage, per the dictionary's collected loci.
variants.arithmetic: The count restarts at the boundary event: '1 KASKAL.GÍD ūmu' counts from sunrise, '1 KASKAL.GÍD GE₆' counts from sunset. A continuous 1→12 cycle from a single daily epoch is NOT attested; if an engine implements one, that is a modern reconstruction and must be labelled as such.

goldenValues.label: GV-1 — Length of day and night in UŠ, 15th of each month, ideal 360-day calendar, 2:1 scheme (PUBLISHED TABLE, exact)
goldenValues.place: none — the scheme is latitude-free schematic arithmetic and specifies no observing site
goldenValues.date: 15th of Months I–XII of the ideal 360-day calendar (equinoxes at 15/I and 15/VII, solstices at 15/IV and 15/X)
goldenValues.expected: day/night in UŠ — I: 180/180; II: 200/160; III: 220/140; IV: 240/120; V: 220/140; VI: 200/160; VII: 180/180; VIII: 160/200; IX: 140/220; X: 120/240; XI: 140/220; XII: 160/200. Every row sums to 360 UŠ. Equivalent in bēru: divide by 30 (IV = 8 bēru day / 4 bēru night). Equivalent in modern hours: multiply UŠ by 4 minutes.
goldenValues.publishedIn: J. M. Steele, 'Shadow-Length Schemes in Babylonian Astronomy', SCIAMVS 14 (2013) 3–39, Table 1 at p. 5 (columns headed '2:1'). Printed there in Babylonian sexagesimal place notation: 3,0 = 180; 3,20 = 200; 3,40 = 220; 4,0 = 240; 2,40 = 160; 2,20 = 140; 2,0 = 120.

goldenValues.label: GV-2 — Same table, 3:2 scheme (PUBLISHED TABLE, exact)
GV-3 — MUL.APIN's own statement, in minas of water, at the four cardinal days (PUBLISHED PRIMARY TEXT, exact)
goldenValues.expected: whole daytime / whole night, in minas: 15/I = 3 / 3; 15/IV = 4 / 2; 15/VII = 3 / 3; 15/X = 2 / 4. The nychthemeron is always 6 minas, so 1 mina = 60 UŠ = 2 bēru = 4 modern hours. NOTE the reading: 'watch' here means the whole daytime or whole night, NOT a third (see variants[v-massartu-sense]).
goldenValues.publishedIn: MUL.APIN II ii 21, 25, 31, 35, in the edition of H. Hunger, in Hunger & Pingree, MUL.APIN: An Astronomical Compendium in Cuneiform (AfO Beiheft 24; Horn: Berger & Söhne, 1989); the four lines are reproduced with translation and commentary in Steele, SCIAMVS 14 (2013) 7–8. Hunger's edition is in copyright and is cite-only under FRAMING §4; the numerals are reported here as data, not as reproduced text.

goldenValues.label: GV-4 — Unit arithmetic (PUBLISHED, exact, no astronomy required)
goldenValues.expected: 1 bēru = 30 UŠ; 1 UŠ = 60 NINDA; daylight + night = 360 UŠ = 24 h. Therefore 1 bēru = 120 min exactly, 1 UŠ = 4 min exactly, 1 NINDA = 4 s exactly, and 12 bēru = 360 UŠ = 21600 NINDA = 86400 s. Also: 1 bēru = 30° of arc, 1 UŠ = 1° of arc.
goldenValues.publishedIn: Steele, SCIAMVS 14 (2013) 4 ('The length of day and night on any day of the year must add up to 360 UŠ (= 24 hours) … bēru and UŠ (1 bēru = 30 UŠ)'; 'there are 30 UŠ in a bēru and 60 NINDA in an UŠ', p. 8). Arc meanings: CAD B 208 and 211 s.v. bēru A mngs. 1 and 3.

goldenValues.label: GV-5 — The equinoctial 6+6 bēru, from a Neo-Assyrian letter (PUBLISHED PRIMARY ATTESTATION)
goldenValues.place: Assyria — the Nineveh scholarly correspondence; no observing site is named in the letter
goldenValues.date: 15 Nisannu (Month I day 15), year not stated
goldenValues.expected: On the 15th of Nisannu day and night were equal: six double-hours of daylight, six double-hours of night. In UŠ: 180 / 180. This is the only place in the entries where the 6+6 split holds.
goldenValues.publishedIn: ABL 1428:4 (cf. ABL 1429:4) — R. F. Harper, Assyrian and Babylonian Letters Belonging to the Kouyunjik Collections of the British Museum (Chicago, 1892–1914), no. 1428, line 4; quoted with translation at CAD B 211 s.v. bēru A mng. 2b. Harper's ABL is public domain in the United States (published 1892–1914, well before the 1930 threshold).

goldenValues.label: GV-6 — The ziqpu circle: 12 bēru, and the 364 UŠ anomaly (PUBLISHED, exact)
goldenValues.place: Babylonia (AO 6478 is Late Babylonian; K 9794 is its Neo-Assyrian near-duplicate from Nineveh)
goldenValues.date: n/a — a star list, not a dated observation
goldenValues.expected: STT 340 and BM 38369+ describe the ziqpu-stars as amounting to 12 bēru; at 30 UŠ per bēru that is 12 × 30 = 360 UŠ, matching the 360-UŠ nychthemeron and the 1-UŠ-per-day schematic calendar. AO 6478's own summation line, however, totals 364 UŠ, i.e. 12 bēru and 4 UŠ.
goldenValues.publishedIn: F. Thureau-Dangin, 'Distances entre étoiles fixes d'après une tablette de l'époque des Séleucides', Revue d'Assyriologie 10 (1913) 215–225 (editio princeps of AO 6478; public domain, published 1913); discussed at G. Breger, 'Ziqpu-stars and Cuneiform Knowledge' (PhD diss., UC Berkeley, 2022) 20 and 29–30, with the competing explanations of Horowitz (1998) 184–85, Hunger & Pingree (1999) 86, Koch (1997) and Steele (2017) 15–16.

derivedNotPublished.warning: The following is ARITHMETIC THIS DOSSIER PERFORMED on GV-1. It is not a published table and no cuneiform text states it. It is offered only so an engine test can check internal consistency; it must never be presented on the page as an attested Babylonian value.
derivedNotPublished.watchLengthsUnder2to1: If a night watch is one third of the schematic night, then at 15/IV the night is 120 UŠ and a watch is 40 UŠ = 2 h 40 m; at 15/I and 15/VII the night is 180 UŠ and a watch is 60 UŠ = 2 bēru = 4 h; at 15/X the night is 240 UŠ and a watch is 80 UŠ = 5 h 20 m.
derivedNotPublished.whyItIsNotAttested: No source seen here combines the schematic day-length scheme with the three-fold watch division to produce watch lengths. The schemes that give lengths use 'watch' to mean the whole of day or night (variants[v-massartu-sense]); the texts that use three watches give no lengths. Joining them is a modern move.

polarBehaviour:
THE TWO HALVES BEHAVE COMPLETELY DIFFERENTLY, AND THAT IS THE INTERESTING RESULT.

(1) The bēru does not break anywhere. It is a fixed twelfth of the mean solar day — 2 hours, always, at every latitude, in every season. There is no polar failure mode for the unit itself. What DOES break is its attested anchoring: the counts are 'n double-hours after sunrise' and 'n double-hours of the night', and above the Arctic and Antarctic circles there are stretches with no sunrise and no sunset, so the anchor vanishes even though the unit survives. An engine may keep counting bēru from local mean midnight or from any chosen epoch, but that epoch is the engine's choice and must be labelled as such (see variants[v-beru-anchor]).

(2) The maṣṣartu does break. A watch is one third of the actual daylight or of the actual night, so during polar day the three night watches have zero length and during polar night the three day watches have zero length; at the transition they are degenerate rather than merely long. There is no attested Babylonian rule for this case, because the question could not arise. The honest render is an empty cell reading 'not attested in this witness', not a fallback.

(3) The schematic schemes are not latitude models at all and must not be evaluated at other latitudes as though they were. The 2:1 ratio is, in Steele's words, very inaccurate for the latitude of Babylon or anywhere else in Babylonia or Assyria; it is an arithmetical framework, not a measurement of a place. Feeding a user's own city into the 2:1 or 3:2 zigzag produces numbers that are correct for nowhere. If the page offers the schematic scheme at all, it should offer it as a fixed table, not as a function of the user's latitude.

gaps: NO RULER, ANYWHERE. Not one of the sources read here — the dictionary entries with their several hundred collected loci, the Diviner's Manual, the hemerology, the eclipse reports, MUL.APIN, the ziqpu lists, the letters — assigns a planet, a god, a demon or any other ruling power to a bēru or to a watch. This is a CONFIRMED NEGATIVE, not an unsearched field: bēru A, barārītu, qablītu, šāt urri, namāritu, maṣṣartu, šēru, muṣlālu and lilâtu were all read in full in the CAD. The Babylonian row of the comparison page must have an empty ruler column, and the page must say why it is empty rather than leaving the reader to infer an oversight.

NO NAMES FOR INDIVIDUAL BĒRU. The watches have names; the double-hours do not. They are referred to only as ordinals counted from sunrise or sunset. Anyone who has seen a list of twelve named Babylonian double-hours has seen a modern invention.

NO CONTINUOUS 1→12 BĒRU CYCLE IS ATTESTED. The counts restart at the boundary event. If the engine renders a single twelve-cell strip from sunset to sunset it is presenting a modern reconstruction; that must be labelled.

ROCHBERG-HALTON 1989, 'Babylonian Seasonal Hours', COULD NOT BE OBTAINED (Wiley 403, Brill 403). That paper is the field's dedicated treatment of exactly the question this dossier is being asked — whether Babylonia had anything answering to a seasonal hour. Its conclusions are therefore NOT represented here, and any claim this dossier makes about the absence of a Babylonian seasonal hour is provisional pending it.

NO WATCH → LAND SCHEME COULD BE COMPLETED. 'The morning watch concerns Elam' is attested twice (Thompson Rep. 242 rev. 2; ACh Supp. 2 Sin 19:13) and paraphrased a third time (Thompson Rep. 181:6). No corresponding land was found for the evening or the middle watch in any entry read. The four-lands scheme (Akkad, Elam, Amurru, Subartu) is well attested for the QUADRANTS OF THE ECLIPSED MOON and for eclipse COLOURS; whether it also ran over the three watches is not established here. DO NOT complete this row by inference — that is precisely FRAMING §5 A-2.

NO PUBLISHED BABYLONIAN TABLE OF REAL WATCH BOUNDARIES FOR A REAL PLACE AND DATE EXISTS in anything read here. Every published table is either schematic (2:1 / 3:2, latitude-free) or a single observational datum in a letter. So there is no golden value against which to test an engine that computes actual sunrise/sunset thirds. Any such computation is the site's own, and the page must say so.

KAR 177 iii 38–39 WAS NOT READ IN THE ORIGINAL. The two half-lines that give the watch qualities were taken from two different CAD volumes; Ebeling's copy and Labat's edition (Hémérologies et ménologies d'Assur, 1939) were not consulted. The values are reported with that caveat.

THE DAY-WATCH QUALITIES ARE MISSING FROM THE RECORD, not from this dossier. Oppenheim's n. 42 states that the duplicate K.6476, which is the tablet that lists the three day watches, does not indicate their favourable or unfavourable character, and that the two versions of the manual disagree about the qualities of the night watches. The day-watch quality cells are therefore genuinely empty.

NO SUBDIVISION OF A WATCH IS ATTESTED. The bēru divides into UŠ and NINDA; the watch does not appear to divide into anything. Whether a Babylonian could say 'the second third of the middle watch' is not established here.

THE ZIQPU INTERVAL LIST WAS NOT TRANSCRIBED. Breger 2022 was read for the totals (12 bēru, 360 UŠ, the 364 anomaly) but the full star-by-star interval table of AO 6478 was not extracted and is not in this dossier. It is available in Thureau-Dangin RA 10 (1913) 215–225, which is public domain and not obtained.

PROVENANCE OF THE 2:1 RATIO IS UNEXPLAINED. It is not Babylon's latitude and no source read here says what latitude, if any, it does correspond to. This dossier deliberately does NOT compute one: producing '≈49°N' from the 16-hour longest day would be the site manufacturing a number that carries an implication (a northern origin) that no cited scholar has made.
contestedPoints: WHAT 'WATCH' MEANS IN MUL.APIN. Current reading (Gehlken 1991; Brown, Fermor and Walker 1999–2000; Steele 2013): EN.NUN/maṣṣartu in the MUL.APIN day-length and shadow-length statements denotes the WHOLE of the daytime or the WHOLE of the night. Superseded reading (Neugebauer 1975; Pingree in Hunger–Pingree 1989 and, modified, in Hunger–Pingree 1999): it denotes one THIRD. This is not a nuance — it changes every number by a factor of three and it is the difference between a scheme that closes at 360 UŠ and one that does not. A human must rule on whether the page reports both or reports the current reading with the older one in a note.

WHEN THE 3:2 RATIO ARRIVED. Brown, Fermor and Walker (1999–2000): the eighth century BC. Steele (2013): the earliest actual evidence is BM 29371, late sixth century, and an earlier date should not be assumed. Both positions stand; neither is resolved here.

WHAT HERODOTUS MEANT BY 'THE TWELVE PARTS OF THE DAY' (II.109). If he meant the twelve bēru of the nychthemeron, he is describing this system and the Greek debt is real. If he meant twelve seasonal daylight hours, he is describing an Egyptian scheme and has attributed it to the wrong nation. This dossier could not read the modern discussion (Neugebauer, A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy, 1975, and Rochberg-Halton 1989 were both unobtainable) and therefore records the ambiguity without adjudicating it. Note the shape of the problem: the bēru is FIXED and the Greek hour is SEASONAL, so the two candidate referents are not merely different labels for the same thing.

THE 364 UŠ OF AO 6478. Horowitz (Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography, 1998, 184–85) reads it as real, reflecting knowledge of a 364-day stellar year as early as the seventh-century Nineveh duplicate K 9794, and makes it the ancestor of the 364-day calendar of the Apocrypha and the Qumran corpus. Steele (Rising Time Schemes, 2017, 15–16) reads it as a scribal summation error arising from the Rear Twin entry, and reconstructs 360. Koch (1997) and Hunger & Pingree (1999, 86) offer further accounts. Breger (2022) finds Steele convincing. All positions must stand; the Qumran connection in particular is a large claim resting on a four-unit discrepancy.

WHETHER BABYLONIA HAD A SEASONAL HOUR AT ALL. Rochberg-Halton devoted an article to the question and this dossier could not read it. Until someone does, the safest statement the page can make is the narrow one that IS established: the bēru is fixed, the maṣṣartu is seasonal, and no term meaning 'one twelfth of the daylight' was encountered in any lexical entry read.

WHETHER THE WATCHES WERE EXACT THIRDS OR OBSERVATIONALLY JUDGED. Smith (1969) and Steele (2020) both describe them as thirds of the actual light and dark. No cuneiform text read here states the rule of division, and none gives a watch a length. 'One third' may be the modern description of a practice that was in fact a guard rota judged by eye or by star. A human should decide whether the engine may draw hard watch boundaries at all, or should draw them as bands.

THE 'CHALDEAN ORDER' NAME. The repository's own planetary-hours engine is documented as 'Chaldean unequal hours'. That name is a Greek and Roman claim about where the scheme came from; it is not a Babylonian attestation, and nothing in the cuneiform record read here corresponds to it. Whether the comparison page keeps the traditional label, and how it annotates it, is an editorial decision a human must make — but the page must not let the label imply that this dossier found a Babylonian planetary hour, because it did not.
honestLimits:
What this system cannot legitimately claim, in the page's own voice.

This row has no hour lords. The Babylonian sources divide time with great precision and assign no ruler to any of the divisions they make. The empty ruler column is the finding, not a hole in it. Where the comparison page shows Saturn against the first hour of a Saturday, the Babylonian column shows nothing, and it shows nothing because there is nothing there to show.

The planetary hour is not Babylonian. The scheme in which each hour of the day is governed by a planet in descending Chaldean order is a Hellenistic construction, and the word 'Chaldean' in its name is a Greek and Roman claim about origins rather than a Mesopotamian attestation. This site's own planetary-hours engine implements that later scheme; putting it beside the bēru is a comparison of two unrelated things, and the page should say so plainly rather than let adjacency imply descent.

The bēru is not an hour. It is a metrological unit of exactly two modern hours that does the same work for time, arc and distance, and it does not stretch or shrink with the season. Calling it a 'double-hour' is a translator's convenience. It cannot be lengthened at midsummer and it cannot be counted round a dial.

The watch is not a bēru. Day and night were each divided into three seasonally varying watches by a completely separate scheme, and the two only coincide at the equinox. Nesting them, or dividing a watch into bēru, would be an arrangement no Babylonian ever made.

The schematic schemes are not a model of the sky at your city. The 2:1 ratio does not fit the latitude of Babylon, let alone anywhere else; it is arithmetic, not measurement. If the page lets a reader put their own coordinates into it, the numbers that come out are about the scheme and not about the reader's horizon.

Where this page computes real watch boundaries from real sunrise and sunset, it is doing something no surviving Babylonian table does. That computation is the site's, not the tradition's. No published Babylonian table of watch boundaries for a stated place and date is known to this compiler, so there is nothing to check it against, and the page should not present it as a reconstruction of what a Babylonian scribe would have written.

And nothing here is a claim about what any of it does. The hemerology says the morning watch is propitious and the evening watch is not; this page records that the hemerology says so. The eclipse reports say the morning watch concerns Elam; this page records that the reports say so. These are statements about a corpus of omen literature and about nothing else.
